sections.b: Psalm 35 is the longest curse psalm in Book I. A man falsely accused (Psalm 35:11) asks God to take up his case and fight for him, and asks that his attackers be shamed and driven like chaff, with the LORD's angel chasing them down a dark, slippery path (Psalm 35:4–8). What gives the curses their heat is betrayal: he had fasted and mourned for these men when they were sick (Psalm 35:13–14). He does no harm himself; each section ends with a vow to praise God when he is cleared (Psalm 35:9–10, 18, 27–28).

sections.h: "So that I can pay them back" (Psalm 41:10)
sections.b: The sick man of Psalm 41 asks God to raise him up "so that I can pay them back" (Psalm 41:10). If he is a king, repayment may be lawful justice on traitors; if not, it is the raw wish for revenge, which the psalms do not hide. Christian readers set it beside Romans 12:17–21.

sections.h: Four ways churches and synagogues have handled the curses
sections.b: (1) Leave them out of public prayer, as the Roman Liturgy of the Hours does with Psalms 58, 83 and 109 and some verses elsewhere. (2) Pray them against spiritual enemies, as Orthodox monastic tradition does. (3) Pray them in Christ, who bore the curse and prayed for his enemies (Bonhoeffer). (4) Pray them honestly as handing vengeance to God, which breaks the cycle of violence (Zenger; compare C. S. Lewis, Reflections on the Psalms).

common: Christians often avoid the curse psalms in public worship or soften them.
uncommon: Some scholars argue the curse psalms are a nonviolent form of protest, since they give vengeance to God.

sections.b: Book I's last psalms show the range of titles. Psalm 32 is the first called a maskil, a word of uncertain meaning (teaching song or skillful song). Psalm 33 has no Hebrew title at all, though the Greek gives it "Of David" and the Qumran scroll 4QPs-q, as reported, a heading of its own. Psalm 34 ties itself to David at Gath but names the king Abimelech, not Achish (1 Samuel 21:10–15). Psalm 36 calls David "the servant of the LORD", as Psalm 18 does. Psalm 38 is "to bring to remembrance", perhaps tied to the memorial portion of an offering. Psalm 39 is "for Jeduthun", one of David's chief musicians.

sections.b: Book I closes with a run of laments, thanksgivings and wisdom psalms, nearly all "of David". Two are alphabet poems (Psalms 34 and 37). Psalm 40:13–17 is repeated as Psalm 70. Psalm 41 begins with "Happy", as Psalm 1 does, and verse 13 is the doxology that closes the first of the five books: "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from the ages past to the ages to come. Amen and Amen" (Psalm 41:13). The same kind of blessing ends Books II, III and IV (Psalm 72:18–19; Psalm 89:52; Psalm 106:48).
sections.refs: Psalm 34:1–22; Psalm 37:1–40; Psalm 40:13–17; Psalm 41:1; Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18–19; Psalm 89:52; Psalm 106:48

sections.b: Psalm 40:13–17 reappears as Psalm 70, inside the Elohistic Psalter. Where Psalm 40 says "the LORD" (YHWH) in 40:13 and 40:16, Psalm 70 has "God" (Elohim) in 70:1 and 70:4, the pattern seen in Psalms 42–83. Other small changes go the other way (70:5 has "LORD" where 40:17 has "my God"), so the editing was not entirely mechanical.

Psalm 31 swings twice from panic to trust; Psalm 35 is the plea of an accused man; Psalm 38 is a sick man's confession; Psalm 39 is a lament with no turn to praise; Psalm 40:11–17 is a fresh cry right after thanksgiving; Psalm 41 combines sickness and betrayal. They show the lament's parts: address, complaint, request, statement of trust, and vow of praise.

These psalms celebrate God's hesed as wonder (Psalm 31:21), as a wall around the one who trusts (Psalm 32:10), as filling the earth (Psalm 33:5), as reaching the heavens (Psalm 36:5) and as sheltering "the children of Adam" under God's wings (Psalm 36:7). The faithful who answer it are his chasidim (Psalm 31:23; Psalm 37:28).
sections.refs: Psalm 31:7; Psalm 31:21; Psalm 32:10; Psalm 33:5; Psalm 33:18; Psalm 36:5–10; Psalm 40:10–11

sections.h: "Sacrifice and grain offering you did not want" (Psalm 40:6)
sections.b: Psalm 40:6 names four kinds of offering and says God did not want them; instead, "ears you have dug for me". Like 1 Samuel 15:22 and the prophets (Hosea 6:6; Jeremiah 7:22–23), it puts listening and obedience first. Hebrews 10:5–10 quotes the Greek form, "a body you prepared for me", and reads it as Christ's offering of himself, which ends the need for animal sacrifice. Jewish interpreters read it as setting priorities within the temple's worship, not abolishing it.
sections.refs: Psalm 40:6–8; 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Jeremiah 7:22–23; Hebrews 10:5–10; Psalm 51:16–17

sections.b: Psalm 32 tells what silence about sin did ("my bones were wearing out") and what confession did: "you lifted away the guilt of my sin" (Psalm 32:5). Psalm 38 is a sick man's confession: "For I tell about my guilt; my sin fills me with worry" (Psalm 38:18). With Psalms 6, 51, 102, 130 and 143 they make up the seven penitential psalms of Christian tradition, first listed by Cassiodorus.

Paul quotes Psalm 32:1–2 beside Genesis 15:6, joined by the verb "count": God counted Abraham's faith as righteousness, and does not count David's sin. Lutheran and Reformed readers find here righteousness credited apart from works; Catholic and Orthodox readers stress that the same psalm requires confession and teaches a changed life (Psalm 32:5; Psalm 32:8–10).

"The heavens were made by the LORD's word, all their starry army by the breath of his mouth" (Psalm 33:6). Psalm 33 sums up Genesis 1: God speaks, and it is (Psalm 33:9). He also gathers and stores the sea (Psalm 33:7). Christians, from Irenaeus on, read "word" and "breath" with John 1:1–3 and Genesis 1:2.
Psalm 33 praises the LORD's word as upright and faithful (Psalm 33:4), the power that made the heavens (Psalm 33:6), and the plan that outlasts the nations' plans (Psalm 33:10–11).

Psalm 33 calls for thanks "on the lyre" (kinnor) and music on "a ten-string harp" (nevel), played well and with loud shouts. It is the first psalm to call for a "new song" (Psalm 33:3; compare Psalm 40:3). Psalm 39's title names Jeduthun, one of the temple's chief musicians.

sections.h: Telling it in the great gathering (Psalm 40:9–10)
sections.b: Thanksgiving in Israel was public. The rescued poet of Psalm 40 brings "the good news of righteousness to the great gathering" and will not keep God's loyal love hidden (Psalm 40:9–10). Psalm 35:18 and Psalm 22:22 promise the same. Book I ends with the people's "Amen and Amen" (Psalm 41:13).

sections.h: Wisdom psalms at the end of Book I
sections.b: Psalm 34:11–22 becomes a teacher's lesson ("Come here, children"), and Psalm 37 is an alphabet of proverbs from an old man (Psalm 37:25). Psalm 32:8–10 and Psalm 39:4–6 add wisdom reflection to prayer. Their themes, the fear of the LORD, guarded speech, patience and the brevity of life, are those of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes.

Psalm 37 states the classic teaching most fully: the wicked will soon dry up, and the humble will possess the land (Psalm 37:2; Psalm 37:11). It admits that the wicked prosper for now (Psalm 37:7; Psalm 37:35) and asks for patience. Its old man's testimony (Psalm 37:25) is balanced in the Psalter by Psalm 73 and in the Bible by Job.

sections.h: "The humble will take possession of the land" (Psalm 37)
sections.b: Psalm 37 uses Deuteronomy's phrase "take possession of the land" five times (Psalm 37:9, 11, 22, 29, 34), but gives the land to the humble and the waiting rather than to the strong. Jesus' beatitude in Matthew 5:5 takes up verse 11 in its Greek form ("the earth"). The Qumran pesher on Psalm 37 applied it to "the congregation of the poor".

The angel of the LORD appears in only two places in Psalms, side by side: he "pitches camp around those who fear him" (Psalm 34:7), and he drives the enemies like chaff and chases them (Psalm 35:5–6).

sections.h: The poor and needy in Psalms 34–41
sections.b: "Here was a poor man who called out" (Psalm 34:6); God rescues "the poor and needy from those who rob them" (Psalm 35:10); the wicked string their bows "to knock down the poor and the needy" (Psalm 37:14); the rescued king or worshiper calls himself "poor and needy" (Psalm 40:17); and Psalm 41:1 blesses the one who pays attention to the weak, which the Talmud reads as visiting the sick.

sections.h: Sickness and the shortness of life (Psalms 38–39)
sections.b: Psalm 38 describes a body racked by illness and a sufferer abandoned by friends, who reads his pain as discipline for sin. Psalm 39 asks God to teach the shortness of life: "Every human being is only a puff of air" (Psalm 39:11). Neither psalm explains suffering; both bring it to God.

The wicked are to be "silenced, down to Sheol" (Psalm 31:17), and the poet of Psalm 39 asks for relief "before I go away and am no more" (Psalm 39:13). Both reflect the older Israelite view of the dead as silent and cut off, which later texts move beyond.

By the 300s Psalm 34 was sung as people received communion; Cyril of Jerusalem tells the newly baptized that the singer invites them, "Taste and see that the Lord is good". 1 Peter 2:3 had already applied the verse to Christians tasting the Lord's goodness.

The poet asks God to treat him as a host treats a guest: "For I am a foreigner with you, a lodger, as all my fathers were" (Psalm 39:12). The same words describe Israel on God's land (Leviticus 25:23) and David's prayer (1 Chronicles 29:15).

sections.h: The law in the heart (Psalms 37 and 40)
sections.b: "The law of his God is in his heart" (Psalm 37:31), and "your law is in my very core" (Psalm 40:8): two psalms describe a person whose obedience comes from inside, the hope of Deuteronomy 6:6 and Jeremiah 31:33.

sections.h: The righteous sufferer read as Christ (Psalms 31–41)
sections.b: The New Testament reads several lines of these psalms at Jesus' passion: "Into your hand I place my spirit" (Psalm 31:5; Luke 23:46), "not a single one gets broken" (Psalm 34:20; John 19:36), "those who hate me for no reason" (Psalm 35:19; John 15:25), and the friend "who ate my bread" (Psalm 41:9; John 13:18). Hebrews 10:5–7 puts Psalm 40:6–8 in Christ's mouth. Jewish readers answer that these are prayers of David and of any faithful sufferer, which Christians apply to Jesus.
sections.refs: Psalm 31:5; Psalm 34:20; Psalm 35:19; Psalm 40:6–8; Psalm 41:9; Luke 23:46; John 19:36; John 15:25; John 13:18; Hebrews 10:5–7

sections.h: The friend who ate my bread (Psalm 41:9)
sections.b: Readers who follow the psalm titles have long linked the betraying friend of Psalm 41:9 with Ahithophel, the counselor who joined Absalom (2 Samuel 15:12; 2 Samuel 15:31). John 13:18 applies the verse to Judas.
Jeduthun, named with Asaph and Heman in Chronicles, appears in the titles of Psalms 39, 62 and 77. Psalm 39 is "for Jeduthun"; the others say "according to Jeduthun", which may name a style or tune.

Psalm 36 sets the self-deceived wicked man beside those who drink from God's river of delights. Psalm 37 contrasts the wicked who borrow and wither with the righteous who give and endure. Both continue the two ways of Psalm 1.

sections.h: A prayer for night and for death (Psalm 31:5)
sections.b: "Into your hand I place my spirit" (Psalm 31:5) is said in the Jewish bedtime prayers and is taken up in the last stanza of the hymn Adon Olam; in the church it is the responsory of Compline. Jesus prays it on the cross (Luke 23:46).
